verdict: Not quite: the action list, the agent door and /v1 are sound and the gates hold, but four things are confirmed broken for an API-only owner: the owner's own POST /actions call cannot cancel an operation and its failures pause every agent (20-desired.mjs:131, 07-jobs.mjs:64), an owner-only question raised outside a chat hands back choice ids nobody can ever press (17-changes.mjs:95), and a route that throws leaves no trace anywhere (24-handler.mjs:696-699). Fix those first with the small versions, then add the terminal `call` command with the header hint, the two missing verbs (download, forget), the audit and safety reads, and the missing tests for the brain routes, /actions callers and the /v1 strip. Of the 31 findings about a third are copies of each other (error codes three times, the terminal command four times, the route list three times), and the larger builds (update_console, a keyed agent on a Spark, watchdog put-back) are real gaps but need the owner's yes as rule changes rather than being fixes for this pass.

kept.title: Waiting on a long operation is a caller-side loop, breaks across a console restart, and test_changes is not safe to repeat
kept.gap: wait_operation returns as soon as the step text changes and waits at most 45 s (service/src/18-workflows.mjs:224-229). Every caller must write its own loop, and tools/spark.mjs has none: its auto-wait is only for ask_sparkie (lines 131-134). Operations live only in memory (service/src/07-jobs.mjs:2), so after an update, undo_update or a watchdog restart an agent holding an operation id gets 404 'expired' and cannot learn the result by id. The start is written to the fleet record with its id (07-jobs.mjs:13), but wait_operation never looks there. test_changes answers 409 'A test of the changes is running already.' with no operation id (18-workflows.mjs:373), unlike start_model's already-starting, which returns the running operation. tools/console.mjs:81 works around that by searching /jobs.
kept.smallestBuild: Three small changes. (1) Give wait_operation an optional `until: 'done'`: it keeps waiting through step changes up to `seconds`, and the result gains `done: true|false` and `next` (the same call again while not done). (2) When the id is not in `jobs`, look for the last operation event with that id in the fleet record and return { status: 'interrupted' or the recorded end status, note: 'Spark Console restarted since; this is what was recorded.' } instead of 404. (3) Make test_changes return { outcome: 'already', operation: <running id>, next } instead of 409. Tests in test/workflows.test.mjs: a second test_changes returns the same operation id; wait_operation for an id that exists only in events.jsonl returns a status, not 404.

kept.title: A build that crashes after the 45-second check stays broken until someone runs restore.sh by hand
kept.gap: The installer goes back on its own only if the new build does not answer within 45 seconds (deploy/host-on-portal.sh:214-230). After that, an uncaught error ends the process (service/src/25-backup-and-start.mjs:89-91) and systemd starts it again, forever. The watchdog only restarts, at most 3 times an hour, then stops trying (deploy/host-on-portal.sh:249-262); it never puts the last build back, and it writes only to the system log with `logger` (:252, :254), which no action reads (`service_logs` reads the console's unit only, service/worker.py:222). While the console is down every API door is down too, so `undo_update` cannot be called. The owner is not locked out of the Spark, but is locked out of Sparkie and the API until a terminal is used. The planned watchdog rollback (docs/reviews-2026-11-11.md:108-110) is not built.
kept.smallestBuild: In the watchdog script only (deploy/host-on-portal.sh:246-264): the installer writes the install time and snapshot path to `$S/last-install`. When the watchdog reaches its third restart inside an hour and the install is under 24 hours old and `$S/rolled-back-<build>` does not exist, it runs that snapshot's `restore.sh` (files only, never `--with-state`), touches the marker, and appends one JSON line to `$S/watchdog.jsonl` for every restart or put-back. The console reads new lines of that file at start and raises one notice each (covered by F1's start-up line). Test: a shell test in test/ that runs the watchdog script against a fake `systemctl`/`curl` on PATH with three recorded restarts and a fresh `last-install`, and expects restore.sh to be called once and the marker written; a second run does not call it again.

Automatic put-back, if wanted at all, only when systemd reports the unit failed and the build never answered /health once since install, and only with the owner's explicit sign-off as a rule.
kept.why: The gap is real: the installer goes back only inside its 45-second check (deploy/host-on-portal.sh:214-230) and the watchdog only restarts, three times an hour, logging to the system log (:246-262). But an automatic put-back triggered by missed /health answers is risky now that the console is on the internet: anything that can stall or crash it three times within a day of an install would undo that install, security fixes included, which is exactly why undo_update from the internet needs the passkey (18-workflows.mjs:487-492). Changing builds without the owner's yes also sits badly with 'owner approves updates'.
